lesson.title: Rewriting Without Changing Meaning: Factoring, Expanding, and Solving with Confidence
lesson.summary: Build fluency in expanding, factoring, and simplifying algebraic expressions and equations, the symbolic toolkit underneath nearly every ACT algebra question.
lesson.body:
Algebra becomes far less mysterious once you internalize a single idea: every legal manipulation you perform on an expression or equation changes its appearance without changing its value or its truth. Expanding, factoring, combining like terms, and solving for a variable are all just different ways of rewriting the same mathematical statement so it is easier to read, compare, or solve. Fluency here is less about memorizing individual rules and more about recognizing which rewritten form you need for the situation in front of you.

Expanding means distributing multiplication over addition or subtraction, turning a product like 3(x - 4) into 3x - 12. Factoring is the reverse process: starting from an expanded expression and rewriting it as a product. The most common factoring patterns worth having on instant recall are pulling out a greatest common factor (6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)), the difference of squares (a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b)), and trinomial factoring, where x² + bx + c factors into (x + m)(x + n) whenever you can find two numbers m and n that multiply to c and add to b.

Worked example: solving an equation by keeping both sides balanced. Solve for x: 3(x - 4) = 2x + 5. Distribute the 3 on the left side: 3x - 12 = 2x + 5. Subtract 2x from both sides to gather the variable terms together: x - 12 = 5. Add 12 to both sides to isolate x: x = 17. Every step is legal because whatever operation is performed is applied to both sides equally, so the equation stays balanced and true. Check the answer by substituting back into the original equation: 3(17 - 4) = 3(13) = 39 on the left, and 2(17) + 5 = 34 + 5 = 39 on the right. Both sides equal 39, confirming x = 17 is correct.

Worked example: factoring to simplify a rational expression. Simplify (x² - 5x + 6) / (x² - 4). Factor the numerator by finding two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to -5: those numbers are -2 and -3, so x² - 5x + 6 = (x - 2)(x - 3). Factor the denominator as a difference of squares: x² - 4 = x² - 2² = (x - 2)(x + 2). The expression becomes [(x - 2)(x - 3)] / [(x - 2)(x + 2)]. Since (x - 2) appears in both the numerator and denominator, it cancels, leaving (x - 3) / (x + 2). This simplification is only valid where the original denominator is nonzero, so you must also note the restriction x ≠ 2 and x ≠ -2, the second because the simplified denominator would still be zero there, and the first because it was zero in the original, unsimplified expression, even though the factor canceled.

Two habits prevent most algebraic-manipulation mistakes on the ACT. First, when distributing a negative sign or a negative coefficient, apply it to every term inside the parentheses, not just the first one, since dropping a sign on the second term is one of the most common ACT errors. Second, remember that multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number flips the direction of the inequality symbol, a rule that has no equivalent when solving equations and is easy to forget under time pressure.
